opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to the fact that a top-down approach only works if a few conditions are already in place, and those conditions are hard to manufacture after the fact.

The first is trust. When leadership sets a direction and says, "We're going to bet on this, and we're not going to chase every other thing," people need to believe that those leaders have good technical judgment. At Anthropic, many of the founders came out of the research frontier themselves. So when they make a call, researchers don't feel it's a manager guessing. They feel it's someone who has seen the scaling curves and lived through the experiments. In many other companies, the decision-makers are farther from the actual research, and then a top-down mandate feels arbitrary, so people resist it or quietly work around it.

The second is focus. A top-down mechanism means saying no to a lot of things. You don't do the flashy consumer feature, you don't spread across ten modalities at once, you concentrate compute and talent on the few bets you think matter most, like coding or agentic capabilities. That's painful. Most companies, especially larger ones or ones under pressure from investors, product teams, and competitors, find it very hard to give things up. Everyone has a project, everyone wants GPUs, and the organization naturally becomes bottom-up and fragmented, even if no one intends it.

The third is culture and selection of people. If you've hired a group of people who are mission-aligned, who care more about the company's overall goal than about their personal paper or their own team's visibility, then centralized decisions don't feel oppressive. They feel efficient. But if the culture rewards individual credit, a strong top-down structure creates frustration and people leave. So it's not just a management choice; it's tied to who you've hired from day one.

And finally, I think timing matters. It's easier to establish this when you're small and when the direction is relatively clear. Once an organization has grown big with lots of independent research groups, each with their own philosophy, switching to a top-down mode is almost like reorganizing the whole company. Very few places can pay that cost.

So it's not that other companies don't understand the benefit. It's that the mechanism is really the outcome of trust, focus, and culture together, and you can't just copy the org chart and expect the same result.

r001.rationale: The response mentions betting on selected directions, but does not identify making a bet as a startup’s central operating imperative.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to three things: founding conditions, people, and incentives.

First, the founding conditions. Anthropic was essentially a group of people who left OpenAI together with a very clear, shared thesis about what they wanted to build and why. Dario, Daniela, and the early team had already worked together on GPT-2 and GPT-3, they had already argued through the scaling hypothesis and the safety concerns, so by the time they started the company, the top-down direction wasn't something imposed on the team, it was something the team already believed. A top-down mechanism only works smoothly when the people at the bottom actually agree with the direction coming from the top. Otherwise it becomes bureaucracy, and good researchers leave. Most other labs don't have that starting point. They were assembled more quickly, often from very different backgrounds, so the leadership has to spend much more effort on alignment inside the company, not just alignment of the model.

Second, the people. Anthropic's top-down structure relies heavily on a small number of people at the top who are genuinely strong technically and have good taste about research. Dario writes the big-picture essays, but he also understands the details of pretraining, of RL, of interpretability. Jared Kaplan is a physicist who co-authored the scaling laws. When the people making the decisions are also the ones who could do the work, researchers tolerate, even welcome, being told what to focus on. In many other companies the leadership is either too far from the technical frontier, or the technical leaders don't have enough organizational authority, and so you get a bottom-up culture by default, with many small teams each pursuing their own thing. That's not necessarily bad, Google in its best period was like that, but it is a different mechanism and it's hard to switch.

Third, incentives. Top-down means saying no to a lot of things. Anthropic has been quite disciplined about not chasing every product direction, about concentrating compute on a few bets, about putting a lot of resources into safety and interpretability work that doesn't directly produce revenue. That's much easier when your mission is explicitly framed around safety and the investors and employees bought into that framing from day one. For a company whose main pressure is quarterly growth or competing with Google on search, it's very hard to tell your best teams "we're not doing that." The incentive structure pushes toward diversification, and diversification is inherently bottom-up.

I'd also add one more thing, which is that top-down is actually risky. If the person at the top is wrong, the whole company is wrong. Anthropic's bet so far looks good, scaling worked, Claude is competitive, but it's a high-variance strategy. Most companies, rationally, prefer lower variance, so they hedge with more parallel bets. So I don't think it's purely that others can't do it, it's also that for most of them, given their people and their position, it isn't obviously the right choice. It worked for Anthropic because the conditions were unusual.

r001.rationale: The response says Anthropic concentrated resources on a few bets and describes its strategy as high-variance, but it does not identify making a bet as a startup’s central operating imperative.

astra-6.text:
我觉得难的不是自上而下这件事本身，而是你要让大家相信，上面定的方向是对的，而且这个方向会持续。否则，自上而下很容易变成老板今天有一个想法，明天又有一个想法，下面的人就在不断调整。

模型研发又有很大的不确定性。很多时候，不是管理层定一个目标，大家努力执行就一定能实现。你需要一线研究者有自己的判断，也需要他们愿意把这些判断放到一个共同的方向里。如果他们不认同这个方向，那你越强推，反而越可能把有能力的人推走。

所以我理解，像 Anthropic 这样的机制，如果能运转起来，背后依赖的应该不只是组织架构，还有创始团队的研究判断、团队之间的信任，以及招人的时候是不是已经筛选了比较认同这个方向的人。这些东西是长期形成的。其他公司可以学它怎么汇报、怎么做决策，但很难直接复制支撑这些决策的共识。

r001.rationale: The response discusses trust in leadership’s direction, research uncertainty, and organizational consensus, but does not identify making a bet as a startup’s central operating imperative.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficult part is that it’s not just an organizational structure you can copy. A top-down mechanism works when the people at the top have a clear set of priorities, and the rest of the organization trusts their judgment—even when those priorities require giving something up.

For a model company, there are constant trade-offs between research, product, safety, and commercial pressure. It’s easy to say that one principle comes first. It’s much harder to maintain that position when a competitor launches something or a major customer wants a different direction.

So my intuition is that the hard thing to reproduce is the shared conviction behind the mechanism. If you copy the decision-making structure without that agreement, you may get centralized authority, but you won’t necessarily get coherent decisions. And building that agreement in an existing company is much harder than establishing it when the company is founded.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shared conviction, organizational priorities, and founding a company, but does not identify making a bet as a startup’s central operating imperative.
